title: Writing Next Steps That Actually Help
summary: "We'll follow up" isn't a next step. Give it one owner, a visible verb, the evidence to bring back and a clear point to stop, and the work moves the very next morning.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The call ends with "OK, we'll follow up on this." Everyone nods and drops off. The next morning nobody has followed up, and nobody did anything wrong either. That sentence never said who, what or by when. It reads like a plan and works like a mood.

A next step works when someone can start on it without replaying the whole meeting. That takes answers to four short questions: who does it, what exactly do they do, what do they bring back, and where do they stop or hand off? Add a date when the timing matters. Miss one of those and the note can look finished while the work just hangs there.

One name, not "the team"

"Team to check the logs" sounds collaborative. In practice it often means nobody checks them, because everyone assumes someone else will. "Linh checks the failed import logs and pastes two examples into the ticket" gives the work a place to land. A name isn't there to assign blame. It's a handle, so everyone knows who to ask.

Google's research on what makes teams effective points the same way. Two of the five dynamics it found are dependability, where people "reliably complete quality work on time", and structure and clarity, meaning "clear roles, goals, and plans" (Google, Five dynamics of effective teams). Both are hard to have when the last line of the meeting notes is "team to follow up."

A verb you can see

"Investigate the issue" is too wide to start on. Where does it begin? When is it done? Compare:

  • "Reproduce the 500 error on staging with a type-B account."
  • "Check whether the mobile app still calls the old /v1/orders endpoint."
  • "Ask the payment partner whether refunds over 30 days are allowed, and paste their answer in the thread."

Each of these tells the owner what done looks like before they start. A quick test: could someone else tell, just by looking, whether it happened? "Look into it" fails that test. "Reproduce it on staging" passes.

Say what comes back

Evidence keeps a next step from turning into a performance. If the job is to check a risk, what should come back? A screenshot, a log line, a test result, a yes or no, a link to the PR, two sentences in the ticket. Without it, you get "I had a look, seems fine", and the team has no way to tell a careful check from a two-minute glance. With it, anyone can open the ticket and see for themselves.

Put a fence around it

A lot of next steps turn into tunnels with no exit, because nobody said when enough is enough. A stopping point fixes that:

  • Check the last seven days of logs. All the logs ever is a different project.
  • Spike for two hours, then bring back two options.
  • Ask legal for the one sentence we need. Don't ask them to rewrite the policy.

The best stopping points are written as if-then rules. Psychologists call these implementation intentions: "if situation Y comes up, then I'll do Z." A 2006 meta-analysis by Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran pooled 94 independent studies with more than 8,000 participants and found a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65) on reaching a goal, on top of just intending to (Parks-Stamm and Gollwitzer, Goal Implementation). To be fair, those studies looked at people and their own goals, such as studying or exercise, not engineers and tickets. The shape still fits nicely: "If it doesn't reproduce after three tries, post what you tried in the ticket and stop." The owner knows exactly when they're allowed to put it down.

Read them out loud

Before the meeting ends, spend one minute reading the next steps aloud. If anyone can't tell whether a line is theirs, or what "done" means for it, fix it right there. One minute now saves a thread of "wait, who was doing this?" on Thursday.

Bring just enough context

A next step often depends on something the room already settled. If it depends on a decision, link the decision. If the team accepted a trade-off, write it down in one line. If a word means something specific in this project ("active user", "migrated account"), define it once. The person picking it up shouldn't have to rebuild the meeting from someone else's memory. If your notes keep losing that thread, keeping meeting notes close to decisions goes into it in more detail.

Written like a moodWritten like a next step
"We'll follow up with the partner.""An asks the partner by Wednesday whether the sandbox supports refunds and posts their reply in #payments."
"Look into the slow dashboard.""Huy profiles the dashboard query on staging for one hour and shares the three slowest calls."
"Team to review the copy.""Trang reviews the error messages on the signup screen and leaves comments in Figma by Friday."
"Investigate the flaky test.""Minh reruns the checkout test 20 times on CI. If it fails more than twice, he quarantines it and opens a ticket."

One sentence is usually enough

None of this needs a template or a new tool. A next step can be a single line: "Minh reproduces the retry failure on staging by Thursday noon, attaches the request ID and a screenshot to the ticket, and stops after three attempts if it doesn't reproduce." Owner, action, evidence, stopping point and date, all in one sentence that takes fifteen seconds to write.

And it pays off twice. The owner knows exactly what to do. Everyone else knows exactly what to expect, so nobody has to chase anyone.

Try this week

  • Find one "we'll follow up" in your recent notes and rewrite it with a name, a verb and a date.
  • For your next investigation task, write down what comes back: a log line, a screenshot or a yes or no.
  • Add one if-then stopping point to an open-ended task.
  • End your next meeting by reading the next steps aloud.

A next step is the short bridge between talking and doing. Write it clearly enough and the next person can just walk across. When the work is done, closing the loop is the other half of the habit.

faqs.q: What makes a good next step?
faqs.a: It answers four questions: who does it, what exactly they do, what they bring back as evidence, and where they stop or hand off. Add a date when timing matters. If someone can start without replaying the meeting, it's a good next step.

faqs.q: Why shouldn't a next step be assigned to "the team"?
faqs.a: Because everyone assumes someone else will do it. One name gives the work a clear owner and gives everyone else one person to ask. Google's research on effective teams lists dependability and clear roles, goals and plans among the five dynamics that matter.

faqs.q: How do I keep a next step from dragging on?
faqs.a: Give it a stopping point, ideally as an if-then rule: "If it doesn't reproduce after three tries, post what you tried and stop." A 2006 meta-analysis of 94 studies found that if-then plans help people reach their own goals, with a medium-to-large effect (d = 0.65).

faqs.q: Do we need a template for action items?
faqs.a: Usually not. One sentence with an owner, a verb, the evidence, a stopping point and a date is enough. Reading the next steps aloud for a minute before the meeting ends catches most of the vague ones.
